modules.title: Introduction to Computer Networks and Physical Layer

topics.title: OSI 7-LAYER REFERENCE MODEL
topics.sub: Layer Hierarchy, Encapsulation & Protocol Data Units (PDUs)
topics.plain: The OSI model is a 7-floor conceptual building for networking. Each floor has one job: Physical moves raw electrical/optical bits, Data Link hops between direct physical neighbors, Network routes packets across world-wide networks, Transport manages end-to-end reliability, Session manages dialogues, Presentation translates and encrypts formats, and Application is what software interacts with.
topics.def: The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model (ISO/IEC 7498-1) is an architectural framework that divides computer network communication into seven distinct hierarchical layers: Physical (Layer 1, bits), Data Link (Layer 2, frames), Network (Layer 3, packets), Transport (Layer 4, segments/datagrams), Session (Layer 5, dialogues), Presentation (Layer 6, syntax/encryption), and Application (Layer 7, user services).
topics.exam: Memorize Layer PDUs: Layer 1 = Bits, Layer 2 = Frames, Layer 3 = Packets, Layer 4 = Segments (TCP) / Datagrams (UDP), Layers 5-7 = Data / Messages. Routers operate up to Layer 3; standard switches operate at Layer 2.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Do not confuse Session and Presentation layers in TCP/IP. TCP/IP collapses OSI Layers 5, 6, and 7 into a single unified Application layer; Session and Presentation do not exist as independent layers in the TCP/IP stack.
topics.example: When accessing a web application, HTTP data from Layer 7 is converted into ASCII/TLS syntax at Layer 6, tracked across sessions at Layer 5, divided into TCP segments with sequence numbers at Layer 4, addressed with IP headers at Layer 3, packaged into Ethernet frames with MAC addresses at Layer 2, and transmitted as modulated electrical signals over Cat6 copper wire at Layer 1.
topics.q: What are the exact Protocol Data Units (PDUs) handled at Layers 1, 2, 3, and 4 of the OSI model?
topics.a: Layer 1 (Physical) = Bits; Layer 2 (Data Link) = Frames; Layer 3 (Network) = Packets; Layer 4 (Transport) = Segments (TCP) or Datagrams (UDP).

topics.title: OSI VS TCP/IP PROTOCOL SUITE
topics.sub: Theoretical Reference Model vs Practical Internet Architecture
topics.plain: OSI was developed by a standards committee before the code was written, resulting in a clean but rigid theoretical model. TCP/IP was built for ARPANET by researchers writing working software, resulting in a pragmatic 4-layer architecture with the Internet Protocol (IP) acting as the narrow waist connecting everything.
topics.def: The OSI model is a 7-layer formal reference framework maintaining a strict conceptual separation between services, interfaces, and protocols. The TCP/IP model is a 4-layer functional internetworking suite (Network Access, Internet, Transport, Application) characterized by a connectionless Internet layer (IP) and an end-to-end Transport layer supporting both connection-oriented (TCP) and connectionless (UDP) communication.
topics.exam: Key theoretical distinction: OSI supports BOTH connection-oriented and connectionless service at the Network layer, but ONLY connection-oriented service at the Transport layer. TCP/IP supports ONLY connectionless service at the Internet layer, but offers BOTH at the Transport layer.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Many students confuse the pedagogical 5-layer model (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Application) with RFC 1122 TCP/IP. The original TCP/IP specification defines exactly 4 layers, combining Physical and Data Link into the Network Access / Link layer.
topics.example: The global Internet runs on the TCP/IP stack: whether packets travel over Wi-Fi, Ethernet, or 5G, they all converge on IP at the Internet layer, demonstrating the architectural robustness of the IP narrow waist.
topics.q: How do the Network and Transport layers differ in their support for connection-oriented vs connectionless services between OSI and TCP/IP?
topics.a: The OSI Network layer supports both connection-oriented and connectionless services, but its Transport layer is strictly connection-oriented. Conversely, the TCP/IP Internet layer provides strictly connectionless service (IP), while its Transport layer provides both connection-oriented (TCP) and connectionless (UDP) services.

topics.title: DATA ENCAPSULATION AND DECAPSULATION
topics.sub: Header Addition, Header Stripping & Multiplexing Demultiplexing
topics.plain: Encapsulation is like nesting Russian dolls or putting an addressed letter inside progressively larger postal envelopes. As application data travels down the stack, each layer attaches its own header. Decapsulation strips each header off on the way back up at the receiving destination.
topics.def: Encapsulation is the process wherein each descending layer of the protocol stack wraps the incoming higher-layer Service Data Unit (SDU) with its own control information header (and trailer) to produce a Protocol Data Unit (PDU). Decapsulation is the complementary process executed in ascending order at the destination host to unpack the payload.
topics.exam: Encapsulation occurs during transmission (Layer 7 down to Layer 1); Decapsulation occurs during reception (Layer 1 up to Layer 7). The Data Link layer is unique because it appends BOTH a header (source/dest MAC) and a trailer (FCS/CRC).
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Intermediate store-and-forward routers do not decapsulate packets all the way to Layer 4; routers decapsulate incoming frames up to Layer 3, inspect the IP destination, rewrite the Layer 2 header for the next hop, and retransmit.
topics.example: An HTTP GET request (L7) is encapsulated with a 20-byte TCP header (L4) specifying destination port 80, wrapped in a 20-byte IP header (L3) with destination IP, and framed by an Ethernet header (L2) with next-hop MAC and 4-byte CRC-32 trailer.
topics.q: Why is the Data Link layer unique among all OSI layers during the encapsulation process?
topics.a: The Data Link layer is the only layer in the OSI stack that attaches both a header (containing source and destination physical MAC addresses) and a trailer (containing the Frame Check Sequence / CRC checksum for error detection) to the PDU.

topics.title: GUIDED VS UNGUIDED TRANSMISSION MEDIA
topics.sub: Twisted Pair, Coaxial Cable, Optical Fiber & Wireless Propagation
topics.plain: Guided media physically confines signals inside a cable: Twisted Pair cancels noise by twisting wires together, Coaxial uses a copper shield against radio interference, and Fiber Optics transmits pulses of light through glass. Unguided media broadcasts electromagnetic waves through air, vacuum, or water without physical conductors.
topics.def: Transmission media provide the physical communication channel between transmitter and receiver. Guided media constrain electromagnetic waves within solid physical boundaries: Twisted Pair (UTP/STP, subject to attenuation and crosstalk), Coaxial Cable (central conductor surrounded by dielectric and braided shield), and Optical Fiber (silica core and cladding operating via Total Internal Reflection, offering massive bandwidth and immunity to EMI). Unguided media radiate radio waves, microwaves, or infrared signals through open space.
topics.exam: Total Internal Reflection (TIR) in optical fiber requires two mandatory conditions: 1) The core refractive index (n1) must be strictly greater than the cladding refractive index (n2); 2) The angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle (theta > theta_c = arcsin(n2/n1)).
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Wires are twisted in twisted-pair cables not for mechanical tensile strength, but to ensure that external electromagnetic interference affects both wires equally, allowing differential receivers to cancel the common-mode noise.
topics.example: Intercontinental Internet backbones utilize single-mode fiber optic cables beneath the ocean, transmitting multi-terabit data streams across thousands of kilometers with optical erbium-doped fiber amplifiers (EDFAs) rather than electrical repeaters.
topics.q: What two physical conditions must be satisfied for light to propagate through an optical fiber via Total Internal Reflection?
topics.a: 1) The refractive index of the core ($n_1$) must be greater than that of the cladding ($n_2$), i.e., $n_1 > n_2$. 2) The angle of incidence at the core-cladding boundary must be greater than the critical angle ($\theta > \theta_c = \arcsin(n_2 / n_1)$).

topics.title: NETWORK TOPOLOGIES & SCOPE CLASSIFICATION
topics.sub: Mesh, Star, Bus, Ring, Tree, Hybrid; LAN, MAN, WAN
topics.plain: Topology is the geometrical map of network connections. Full Mesh connects every node directly to every other node for maximum reliability at high cost. Star connects all nodes to a central switch. Bus shares a single backbone cable. Ring routes data in a circular loop. Networks are also categorized by geographic span: LAN (room/building), MAN (city), and WAN (country/globe).
topics.def: Network topology defines the physical or logical arrangement of links and nodes. A fully connected Mesh requires $n(n-1)/2$ full-duplex physical channels for $n$ devices, providing dedicated links with zero traffic contention and high fault tolerance. Star topology connects all nodes via point-to-point links to a central multi-port hub or switch. Bus uses a multipoint shared cable terminated with resistors. Ring connects devices in a closed daisy chain with repeaters. Geographically: LAN covers < 1 km; MAN covers 5-50 km; WAN spans continental or global distances.
topics.exam: Formulas: Fully connected mesh links = $n(n - 1) / 2$; I/O ports per device = $n - 1$. For 10 nodes, links = $10 \times 9 / 2 = 45$.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: In a Star topology, a failure of a single peripheral cable affects only that node, but failure of the central switch disables the entire network. In a Bus topology, a break anywhere in the backbone cable brings down the whole segment.
topics.example: Modern gigabit enterprise LANs utilize a physical Star topology with twisted-pair Cat6 cables connected to centralized managed switches, while high-availability data center backbones often deploy Clos or Spine-and-Leaf mesh fabrics.
topics.q: How many full-duplex physical links and how many I/O ports per computer are required to build a fully connected physical mesh topology for 12 workstations?
topics.a: Total links = $n(n - 1) / 2 = 12 \times 11 / 2 = 66$ links. Each individual workstation requires $n - 1 = 11$ I/O ports.

topics.title: CIRCUIT SWITCHING VS PACKET SWITCHING
topics.sub: Dedicated Paths vs Store-and-Forward Statistical Multiplexing
topics.plain: Circuit switching is like reserving a private telephone line: bandwidth is reserved in advance, guaranteed, but wasted if you stay silent. Packet switching chops messages into independent packets that share links on demand, maximizing efficiency through statistical multiplexing at the cost of slight queuing delays.
topics.def: Circuit switching establishes a dedicated, reserved end-to-end physical communication channel across intermediate switches for the entire duration of a session (phases: Setup, Data Transfer, Teardown), offering fixed bandwidth and zero queuing delay. Packet switching segments messages into discrete packets that traverse shared links via store-and-forward routing, employing statistical multiplexing for optimal link utilization but incurring queuing delay and jitter.
topics.exam: Circuit switching has zero queuing delay during data transfer, but requires initial call-setup delay. Packet switching has zero setup delay (in datagram mode), but introduces variable queuing delays at intermediate routers.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Datagram packet switching does not guarantee packets arrive in order or follow the same physical route; Virtual Circuit packet switching establishes a pre-planned logical route (VCI) ensuring in-order delivery while still sharing link bandwidth.
topics.example: Traditional landline telephone networks (PSTN) employ circuit switching. The Internet, IP telephony (VoIP), and cellular data networks operate exclusively on packet switching.
topics.q: Why is packet switching fundamentally superior to circuit switching for bursty computer data communication?
topics.a: Packet switching uses statistical multiplexing to allocate link capacity dynamically on demand only when data is actively being sent. Circuit switching dedicates fixed bandwidth for the entire connection duration, wasting substantial capacity during idle periods.

topics.title: TRANSMISSION IMPAIRMENTS & SIGNAL DEGRADATION
topics.sub: Attenuation, Distortion, Thermal Noise & Signal-to-Noise Ratio
topics.plain: Signals lose quality over distance in three ways: Attenuation (signals get weaker like a fading whisper), Distortion (signals change shape because different frequencies travel at different speeds), and Noise (unwanted electrical hum or static added to the signal). We measure signal quality using the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR).
topics.def: Transmission impairments degrade analog and digital signals propagating through physical communication channels: 1) Attenuation: exponential loss of signal amplitude over distance, expressed in decibels ($dB = 10 \log_{10}(P_2 / P_1)$), compensated via amplifiers or repeaters. 2) Distortion: signal waveform shape alteration caused by frequency-dependent phase velocities in composite signals. 3) Noise: external or internal extraneous energy, including thermal noise (Johnson noise, $N = kTB$), crosstalk, and impulse noise. Signal-to-Noise Ratio is $SNR = P_{\text{signal}} / P_{\text{noise}}$, or $SNR_{dB} = 10 \log_{10}(SNR)$.
topics.exam: Formulas: Decibels $dB = 10 \log_{10}(P_{\text{out}} / P_{\text{in}})$. Halving power corresponds to a $-3\text{ dB}$ change ($10 \log_{10}(0.5) \approx -3.01\text{ dB}$). A drop to $1/10$ input power is a $-10\text{ dB}$ loss.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Thermal noise is intrinsic to all conductors operating above absolute zero due to thermal electron agitation and cannot be eliminated; impulse noise is episodic (e.g., machinery, lightning) and causes catastrophic burst errors.
topics.example: Ethernet specifications limit UTP copper cable runs to 100 meters because signal attenuation beyond 100 meters drops signal voltage below the threshold where receivers can reliably discriminate 1s from 0s.
topics.q: If a signal with a power of 50 mW is fed into a transmission line and the measured output power at the receiver is 0.5 mW, what is the attenuation in decibels?
topics.a: Attenuation in dB = $10 \log_{10}(P_{\text{out}} / P_{\text{in}}) = 10 \log_{10}(0.5 / 50) = 10 \log_{10}(0.01) = 10 \times (-2) = -20\text{ dB}$ (a signal loss of 20 dB).

topics.title: NYQUIST BIT RATE & SHANNON CHANNEL CAPACITY
topics.sub: Theoretical Data Rates for Noiseless and Noisy Channels
topics.plain: Nyquist tells you how fast you can push bits through an ideal noiseless channel if you increase the number of signal voltage levels. Shannon tells you the strict physical speed limit of a noisy channel that no engineer can ever exceed, determined purely by channel bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio.
topics.def: Nyquist's Bit Rate formula defines the maximum theoretical transmission rate for a noiseless channel of bandwidth $B$ (Hertz) with $V$ discrete signal levels: $C_{\text{Nyquist}} = 2B \log_2(V)$ bps. Shannon's Capacity theorem defines the theoretical maximum capacity of a channel perturbed by Gaussian white noise with bandwidth $B$ and signal-to-noise ratio $SNR$: $C_{\text{Shannon}} = B \log_2(1 + SNR)$ bps.
topics.exam: Formulas: $C = 2B \log_2(V)$ (Nyquist) and $C = B \log_2(1 + SNR)$ (Shannon). If $SNR$ is given in decibels ($dB$), you MUST convert to a linear power ratio before applying Shannon: $SNR = 10^{(SNR_{dB} / 10)}$.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Never substitute $SNR_{dB}$ directly into Shannon's formula. If an exam problem states $SNR = 30\text{ dB}$, the linear ratio is $10^{30/10} = 1000$, yielding $C = B \log_2(1001)$.
topics.example: A traditional telephone line with bandwidth $B = 3100\text{ Hz}$ and typical $SNR = 30\text{ dB}$ ($SNR = 1000$) has maximum Shannon capacity $C = 3100 \times \log_2(1001) \approx 3100 \times 9.967 \approx 30.9\text{ kbps}$. Dial-up modems reached 56 kbps only by using digital connections at one end.
topics.q: Calculate the theoretical Shannon capacity of a communication channel having a bandwidth of 3 kHz and a Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) of 31.
topics.a: Using Shannon's formula $C = B \log_2(1 + SNR) = 3000 \times \log_2(1 + 31) = 3000 \times \log_2(32) = 3000 \times 5 = 15,000\text{ bps} = 15\text{ kbps}$.

topics.title: NETWORK DELAY COMPONENTS & BANDWIDTH-DELAY PRODUCT
topics.sub: Transmission, Propagation, Queuing, Processing Delays & Link Capacity
topics.plain: Whenever a packet travels across the internet, its journey takes time due to 4 distinct delays: Processing (router reading the header), Queuing (waiting in router line), Transmission (pushing bits onto the wire like pushing cars through a toll booth), and Propagation (speed of light travel time through the cable).
topics.def: Total nodal delay is the sum of four components: $d_{\text{nodal}} = d_{\text{proc}} + d_{\text{queue}} + d_{\text{trans}} + d_{\text{prop}}$. Transmission delay is the time required to push all packet bits onto the link: $d_{\text{trans}} = L / R$ (where $L$ is packet size in bits and $R$ is transmission rate in bps). Propagation delay is the time required for one bit to travel from sender to receiver: $d_{\text{prop}} = d / s$ (where $d$ is distance and $s$ is physical propagation velocity, $\approx 2 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$ in copper/fiber). Bandwidth-Delay Product ($BDP = R \times d_{\text{prop}}$) measures the maximum number of in-flight bits the link pipe can hold.
topics.exam: Key formula distinction: $d_{\text{trans}} = L / R$ is determined by packet length and transmission speed. $d_{\text{prop}} = d / s$ is determined by physical link distance and light velocity. They are completely independent!
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Upgrading a 10 Mbps link to 1 Gbps reduces transmission delay ($L/R$) by a factor of 100, but has zero effect on propagation delay ($d/s$). Bits do not move faster through the glass cable.
topics.example: A geostationary satellite link at 36,000 km altitude has one-way propagation delay $d_{\text{prop}} = 36,000,000 / (3 \times 10^8) = 120\text{ ms}$ (round-trip 240 ms). Even on a 1 Gbps link, interactive voice chat suffers noticeable latency due to propagation delay.
topics.q: A host sends a 1500-byte packet over a 100 Mbps fiber optic link of length 200 km. If signal speed in fiber is $2 \times 10^8$ m/s, what are the transmission and propagation delays?
topics.a: Transmission delay $d_{\text{trans}} = (1500 \times 8\text{ bits}) / (100 \times 10^6\text{ bps}) = 12,000 / 10^8 = 0.00012\text{ s} = 0.12\text{ ms} = 120\ \mu\text{s}$. Propagation delay $d_{\text{prop}} = (200 \times 10^3\text{ m}) / (2 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}) = 0.001\text{ s} = 1\text{ ms}$.

topics.title: MULTIPLEXING: FDM, TDM, WDM & STATISTICAL TDM
topics.sub: Frequency, Time, Optical Wavelength Sharing & Statistical Multiplexing
topics.plain: Multiplexing is combining multiple low-speed data conversations onto a single high-speed shared cable. FDM splits the cable into separate radio frequencies (like FM radio stations). TDM gives each user a turn in a rotating time slot. WDM runs multiple different colors of light down an optical fiber. Statistical TDM dynamically allocates slots only to people who have data right now.
topics.def: Multiplexing is the simultaneous transmission of multiple information signals over a single shared data link: 1) Frequency-Division Multiplexing (FDM): divides analog bandwidth into discrete frequency bands separated by guard bands. 2) Synchronous Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM): assigns recurring fixed time slots to each input line; idle lines waste allocated time slots. 3) Wavelength-Division Multiplexing (WDM): combines optical carrier signals of different wavelengths onto a single optical fiber. 4) Statistical (Asynchronous) TDM: dynamically allocates time slots on demand based on buffer availability, maximizing link utilization for bursty traffic.
topics.exam: Synchronous TDM requires link capacity $C \ge \sum R_i$ (sum of all peak user rates). Statistical TDM allows link capacity $C < \sum R_i$ by relying on the statistical unlikelihood of all bursty users transmitting simultaneously.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: WDM is conceptually identical to FDM, but operates strictly in the optical domain using light wavelengths measured in nanometers rather than electrical frequencies measured in Hertz.
topics.example: Dense Wavelength Division Multiplexing (DWDM) enables modern telecommunication providers to transmit 80 to 160 distinct optical wavelengths over a single pair of fiber strands, achieving aggregate throughputs exceeding 40 Terabits per second.
topics.q: What fundamental inefficiency of Synchronous TDM is resolved by Statistical Time-Division Multiplexing?
topics.a: In Synchronous TDM, if a user has no data to transmit, their assigned time slot is transmitted empty, wasting channel bandwidth. Statistical TDM dynamically assigns slots on demand only to active channels, achieving near 100% link utilization.

quiz.q: Which Protocol Data Unit (PDU) is correctly paired with its corresponding OSI reference model layer?
quiz.correctFb: Layer 2 (Data Link Layer) exchanges Frames, while Layer 3 (Network Layer) exchanges Packets. Layer 1 exchanges Bits and Layer 4 exchanges Segments or Datagrams.
distractors: Inverts the PDUs of Layer 2 and Layer 3.
Segments belong to Layer 4 (Transport) and Packets belong to Layer 3 (Network).
Bits belong to Layer 1 (Physical) and Frames belong to Layer 2 (Data Link).

quiz.q: Regarding support for connection-oriented and connectionless services, what is a fundamental architectural difference between the OSI and TCP/IP models?
opts: OSI supports both connection-oriented and connectionless service at the Network layer, whereas TCP/IP supports only connectionless service (IP) at the Internet layer.
TCP/IP supports only connection-oriented service at both the Internet and Transport layers.
OSI supports only connectionless service at the Transport layer, whereas TCP/IP supports both.
TCP/IP requires connection-oriented virtual circuits at the Network Access layer for all traffic.
quiz.correctFb: The OSI model was designed to accommodate both connection-oriented (X.25 style) and connectionless services at Layer 3. The TCP/IP Internet layer was strictly designed around connectionless datagram delivery (IP), relying on the Transport layer (TCP) for connection-oriented reliability.
distractors: TCP/IP Internet layer is strictly connectionless (IP); Transport supports both TCP and UDP.
OSI Transport layer is strictly connection-oriented (classes TP0 to TP4); it does not allow connectionless transport.
TCP/IP operates over connectionless media like standard Ethernet without requiring virtual circuits.

quiz.q: What physical condition must be satisfied for an optical signal to propagate through the core of an optical fiber via Total Internal Reflection?
opts: Core refractive index must be lower than cladding refractive index, and angle of incidence must be 90 degrees.
Core refractive index must be greater than cladding refractive index, and angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle.
Core and cladding must have identical refractive indices to prevent modal dispersion.
Light must enter perpendicular to the fiber axis with an angle of incidence less than Brewster's angle.
quiz.correctFb: Total Internal Reflection requires that light travel from a medium of higher refractive index to one of lower refractive index ($n_{\text{core}} > n_{\text{cladding}}$) and strike the boundary at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle $\theta_c = \arcsin(n_{\text{cladding}} / n_{\text{core}})$.
distractors: If the core refractive index were lower than cladding, light would refract out into the cladding and attenuate rapidly.
Identical refractive indices would eliminate reflection completely, causing light to leak directly out.
Brewster's angle pertains to polarization upon reflection, not guided optical fiber confinement.

quiz.q: How many full-duplex physical links and how many I/O ports per device are required to connect 10 computers in a fully connected mesh topology?
opts: 45 physical links and 9 I/O ports per device
90 physical links and 10 I/O ports per device
45 physical links and 10 I/O ports per device
10 physical links and 2 I/O ports per device
quiz.correctFb: For $n$ devices in a full mesh, the total number of duplex links is $n(n - 1) / 2 = 10 \times 9 / 2 = 45$. Each device must connect to all other $n - 1$ devices, requiring $10 - 1 = 9$ I/O ports.
distractors: 90 links would represent simplex directional links, and devices require $n-1=9$ ports, not 10.
Computers do not need an I/O port to connect to themselves, so each requires 9 ports, not 10.
10 links with 2 ports per device describes a Ring topology, not a fully connected Mesh.

quiz.q: Which type of network delay is eliminated during the active data transfer phase in a circuit-switched network?
quiz.correctFb: In circuit switching, dedicated physical bandwidth is reserved end-to-end prior to transmission. Because buffers are not shared and no packet contention occurs at intermediate switches, queuing delay during data transfer is completely zero.
distractors: Propagation delay is bounded by the speed of electromagnetic waves and is never zero.
Transmission delay is still required to modulate bits onto the communication line.
Processing delay occurs during initial setup, but queuing delay is the key delay eliminated during data transfer.

quiz.q: A communication channel has a bandwidth of 4000 Hz and a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 15. What is the maximum theoretical channel capacity according to Shannon's theorem?
quiz.correctFb: Using Shannon's formula $C = B \log_2(1 + SNR) = 4000 \times \log_2(1 + 15) = 4000 \times \log_2(16) = 4000 \times 4 = 16,000\text{ bps}$.
distractors: 32,000 bps erroneously multiplies by 8 instead of $\log_2(16) = 4$.
60,000 bps erroneously multiplies bandwidth directly by SNR ($4000 \times 15$).
8,000 bps erroneously computes $\log_2(16) = 2$ instead of 4.

quiz.q: A signal enters a 10-kilometer transmission cable with a power of 100 mW and exits at the receiver with 1 mW. What is the total attenuation of the cable in decibels (dB)?
quiz.correctFb: Attenuation in dB is calculated as $10 \log_{10}(P_{\text{out}} / P_{\text{in}}) = 10 \log_{10}(1 / 100) = 10 \log_{10}(10^{-2}) = 10 \times (-2) = -20\text{ dB}$.
distractors: -10 dB corresponds to a power drop to 1/10 (10 mW), not 1/100.
-100 dB confuses the linear power ratio (100) with the decibel value.
-3 dB corresponds to halving the power (50 mW).

quiz.q: If the transmission bandwidth of a link is quadrupled while the physical cable length and packet size remain constant, what happens to the transmission delay and propagation delay?
opts: Both transmission delay and propagation delay are reduced to one-fourth of their original values.
Transmission delay is reduced to one-fourth; propagation delay remains unchanged.
Propagation delay is reduced to one-fourth; transmission delay remains unchanged.
Transmission delay is quadrupled; propagation delay is reduced.
quiz.correctFb: Transmission delay $d_{\text{trans}} = L / R$ is inversely proportional to bandwidth $R$, so quadrupling bandwidth reduces it to $1/4$. Propagation delay $d_{\text{prop}} = d / s$ depends solely on distance $d$ and medium speed $s$, remaining completely unaffected by bandwidth.
distractors: Propagation delay depends purely on the speed of light in the physical medium, not bandwidth.
Bandwidth has zero influence on the physical transit speed of light through the cable.
Transmission delay decreases as bandwidth increases; it does not quadruple.

quiz.q: According to Nyquist's theorem, what is the maximum data rate for a noiseless channel with a bandwidth of 3000 Hz using 4 discrete signaling levels?
quiz.correctFb: Using Nyquist's theorem: $C = 2B \log_2(V) = 2 \times 3000 \times \log_2(4) = 6000 \times 2 = 12,000\text{ bps}$.
distractors: 6,000 bps calculates $2B$ but forgets to multiply by $\log_2(4) = 2$.
24,000 bps mistakenly multiplies by 4 instead of $\log_2(4) = 2$.
3,000 bps equals the bandwidth $B$ without applying the Nyquist factor $2 \log_2(V)$.

quiz.q: Which multiplexing technique combines multiple light signals of varying wavelengths onto a single optical fiber strand?
quiz.correctFb: Wavelength-Division Multiplexing (WDM) combines optical carrier signals of different wavelengths (colors of laser light) onto a single strand of optical fiber using optical prisms or diffraction gratings.
distractors: FDM operates in the electrical/radio frequency domain, whereas optical fiber multiplexing is termed WDM.
Synchronous TDM divides time into distinct digital slots, not optical wavelengths.
CDMA uses orthogonal mathematical spreading codes, not wavelength separation.

bossChallenges.scenario: [10 MARKS] University Exam Question: Provide an exhaustive theoretical and architectural breakdown of the OSI 7-Layer Reference Model versus the TCP/IP Protocol Architecture. Formally define both models, analyze how protocol data units (PDUs) and control headers transform during encapsulation and decapsulation, evaluate the transmission impairment differences across guided media (twisted pair, coaxial, and optical fiber), and calculate the Shannon channel capacity for a noisy 4 kHz band-limited channel with an SNR of 30 dB.
rubric: Criterion 1 (2.5 Marks): Formal definitions and layer-by-layer architectural comparison between OSI (7 layers) and TCP/IP (4 layers), emphasizing service model divergences at the Network and Transport layers.

Criterion 2 (2.5 Marks): Comprehensive explanation of data encapsulation and decapsulation across all layers, specifying exact PDU terminology (Bits, Frames, Packets, Segments, Messages) and header/trailer operations.

Criterion 3 (2.5 Marks): In-depth comparison of guided transmission media (UTP/STP, Coaxial, and Optical Fiber) covering attenuation, electromagnetic immunity, and Total Internal Reflection conditions.

Criterion 4 (2.5 Marks): Rigorous mathematical derivation of Nyquist bit rate and Shannon channel capacity, including linear SNR conversion from 30 dB (ratio 1000) and step-by-step numerical calculation yielding ~39.87 kbps.

bossChallenges.scenario: [5 MARKS] Practical Problem-Solving Scenario: A multinational enterprise with 12 branch offices requires high-availability interconnectivity. The lead network engineer must evaluate whether to deploy a fully connected physical mesh topology versus a physical star topology with redundant core switches. Calculate the exact physical cabling and port requirements for both architectures, analyze single-point-of-failure risks, and formulate an engineering recommendation.
rubric: Criterion 1 (1.25 Marks): Exact mathematical calculation of physical links and device I/O ports for a 12-node full mesh (66 full-duplex links, 11 ports per device) versus star topology (12 links, 1 port per device).
Criterion 2 (1.25 Marks): Rigorous failure analysis evaluating line-break resilience and blast radius in mesh networks versus switch controller failure in star networks.
Criterion 3 (1.25 Marks): Financial and operational trade-off evaluation covering installation complexity, cabling maintenance costs, and hardware port density limitations.
Criterion 4 (1.25 Marks): Concrete engineering recommendation proposing a hybrid or redundant dual-homed star/spine-leaf architecture for optimal reliability and cost.

topics.title: FRAMING TECHNIQUES & BIT/BYTE STUFFING
topics.sub: Character Count, Byte Stuffing (ESC) & HDLC Bit Stuffing
topics.plain: Framing divides an endless stream of raw physical bits into distinct frames. To tell where a frame begins and ends, protocols use flag bytes or flag patterns like 01111110. If that pattern accidentally appears inside user data, the sender 'stuffs' an extra bit or escape byte so the receiver doesn't cut the frame short.
topics.def: Framing is the Data Link layer function of organizing raw bit streams into recognizable discrete data units (frames) with designated boundaries. Primary mechanisms: 1) Character Count: header specifies frame character length (fragile; a single bit error in count derails all subsequent frames). 2) Byte (Character) Stuffing: frame delimiter flags (e.g., DLE STX / DLE ETX) surround data; occurrences of flag or escape bytes in data are escaped with DLE/ESC bytes. 3) Bit Stuffing: frames begin and end with flag pattern 01111110; whenever the sender encounters five consecutive 1s in data, it unconditionally inserts a 0 bit, which the receiver strips.
topics.exam: Bit Stuffing Rule: Sender inserts a 0 bit after EVERY sequence of five consecutive 1s (011111 -> 0111110). Receiver checks after five consecutive 1s: if next bit is 0, it strips the 0 (it was stuffed); if next bit is 1 and followed by 0, it detects a frame flag (01111110).
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Bit stuffing is performed bit-by-bit regardless of byte boundaries; byte stuffing operates on full 8-bit character boundaries.
topics.example: High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC) and Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) employ bit stuffing with 01111110 flags to transmit arbitrary binary files across serial communication links without premature framing termination.
topics.q: If the data stream 01111110111110 is to be transmitted using HDLC bit stuffing, what is the exact resulting bit pattern transmitted on the link?
topics.a: After every five consecutive 1s, a 0 is inserted: 011111[0]1011111[0]0.

topics.title: CYCLIC REDUNDANCY CHECK (CRC)
topics.sub: Modulo-2 Polynomial Arithmetic, Generator Polynomials & Error Coverage
topics.plain: CRC is mathematical division using XOR instead of subtraction. The sender appends $r$ zeroes to the data, divides by a pre-agreed generator code, and appends the remainder to the frame. The receiver divides the whole frame by the same generator—if the remainder is zero, the frame arrived intact!
topics.def: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) is an error-detecting code based on polynomial division in Galois Field GF(2). Given a data block $M(x)$ and a generator polynomial $G(x)$ of degree $r$: 1) Append $r$ zero bits to $M(x)$ (computing $M(x) \cdot x^r$). 2) Divide $M(x) \cdot x^r$ by $G(x)$ using modulo-2 arithmetic (XOR without carries or borrows). 3) The $r$-bit remainder $R(x)$ is added to $M(x) \cdot x^r$ to produce the transmitted codeword $T(x)$. The receiver divides $T(x)$ by $G(x)$; a non-zero remainder indicates transmission error.
topics.exam: Modulo-2 Arithmetic: $0 \oplus 0 = 0$, $0 \oplus 1 = 1$, $1 \oplus 0 = 1$, $1 \oplus 1 = 0$ (XOR). A generator polynomial $G(x)$ of degree $r$ detects all single-bit errors (if $G(x)$ has $>1$ term), all double-bit errors, all odd numbers of errors (if $(x+1)$ is a factor of $G(x)$), and all burst errors of length $\le r$.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: If the generator polynomial has degree $r$, you must append exactly $r$ zero bits (not $r+1$ bits). A generator of degree 4 (e.g., $x^4 + x + 1$, 5 bits long: 10011) generates an $r = 4$-bit remainder.
topics.example: Ethernet frames append a 4-byte (32-bit) Frame Check Sequence (FCS) calculated using the IEEE 802.3 standard polynomial CRC-32: $x^{32} + x^{26} + x^{23} + x^{22} + x^{16} + x^{12} + x^{10} + x^8 + x^7 + x^5 + x^4 + x^2 + x + 1$.
topics.q: What binary bit sequence corresponds to the CRC generator polynomial $G(x) = x^4 + x^2 + 1$, and how many zero bits are appended to the data message prior to modulo-2 division?
topics.a: The polynomial $G(x) = 1\cdot x^4 + 0\cdot x^3 + 1\cdot x^2 + 0\cdot x^1 + 1\cdot x^0$ corresponds to binary 10101. Because the degree of the polynomial is $r = 4$, exactly 4 zero bits are appended to the data message.

topics.title: PARITY CHECKS & INTERNET CHECKSUM
topics.sub: Single/2D Parity, 1's Complement Addition & Checksum Algorithm
topics.plain: Simple parity adds a single bit to make the count of 1s even or odd—great for catching 1 flipped bit, but completely blind if 2 bits flip. The Internet Checksum adds up 16-bit binary words using 1's complement arithmetic and flips all bits (inverts) at the end.
topics.def: Linear error detection techniques: 1) Simple Parity: appends 1 bit making the total count of 1s even (Even Parity) or odd (Odd Parity); detects any odd number of bit errors, fails on even bit errors. 2) Two-Dimensional (2D) Parity: organizes data into a matrix, computing parity for each row and column; detects all 1-, 2-, and 3-bit errors and corrects single-bit errors (intersection of bad row and column). 3) Internet Checksum (RFC 1071): arranges data into 16-bit integers, sums them using 1's complement arithmetic (end-around carry: carry out from bit 15 is added back to bit 0), and takes the 1's complement (bitwise NOT) of the final sum.
topics.exam: 1's complement addition: If adding two 16-bit words produces a carry-out bit beyond 16 bits, wrap the carry around and add 1 to the least significant bit (LSB). The checksum is the bitwise inverse of the final wrapped sum.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: The Internet Checksum does not detect reordering of 16-bit words or insertion of all-zero words, because addition is commutative ($A + B = B + A$) and adding zero does not alter the sum.
topics.example: IP, TCP, and UDP headers include a 16-bit checksum field. When the receiver computes the 1's complement sum over all 16-bit words including the received checksum, the result must be 0xFFFF (all 1s in 1's complement, representing +0).
topics.q: Why is the Internet Checksum unable to detect an accidental reordering of two 16-bit payload words in an IP packet?
topics.a: Because 1's complement addition is mathematically commutative and associative; the sum of $(A + B)$ is identical to $(B + A)$, so swapping the order of words yields the exact same checksum value.

topics.title: STOP-AND-WAIT ARQ PROTOCOL
topics.sub: Mechanics, Sequence Numbers (0/1), Channel Utilization & Efficiency
topics.plain: Stop-and-Wait is the simplest flow and error control protocol: send one frame, freeze and wait. If an ACK arrives, send the next frame. If a timer expires without an ACK, resend the same frame. It uses 1-bit sequence numbers (0 and 1) to distinguish new frames from duplicates.
topics.def: Stop-and-Wait Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ) is a half-duplex sliding window protocol with sender window size $W_s = 1$ and receiver window size $W_r = 1$. The sender transmits a single frame with an alternating 1-bit sequence number ($0$ or $1$) and starts a retransmission timer. The receiver verifies frame integrity; if valid, it returns an ACK containing the expected next sequence number. Channel efficiency is $\eta = \frac{T_t}{T_t + 2T_p} = \frac{1}{1 + 2a}$, where $T_t = L / R$ is transmission delay, $T_p$ is propagation delay, and $a = T_p / T_t$.
topics.exam: Efficiency formula: $\eta = \frac{1}{1 + 2a}$, where $a = T_p / T_t$. When propagation delay is much larger than transmission delay ($a \gg 1$, e.g., satellite links), Stop-and-Wait efficiency approaches zero.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: If an ACK is lost or delayed, the sender times out and retransmits. Without 1-bit sequence numbers (0 and 1), the receiver would mistakenly treat the retransmitted frame as new data, causing data duplication.
topics.example: TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) over UDP operates on a Stop-and-Wait basis, sending 512-byte blocks and waiting for an individual ACK for each block before transmitting the next.
topics.q: A 1000-bit frame is transmitted over a 1 Mbps satellite link with a one-way propagation delay of 250 ms using Stop-and-Wait. Calculate the channel efficiency $\eta$.

topics.title: GO-BACK-N SLIDING WINDOW ARQ
topics.sub: Pipelined Transmission, Cumulative ACKs & Window Size Constraints
topics.plain: Go-Back-N lets the sender transmit up to $N$ frames without waiting for an ACK. But the receiver is completely stubborn: its window size is 1, so it only accepts frames in exact sequential order. If frame 3 is dropped in transit, the receiver discards frames 4, 5, and 6, forcing the sender to 'go back' and retransmit all of them from 3 onwards.
topics.def: Go-Back-N (GBN) ARQ is a pipelined sliding window protocol. The sender maintains a window of size $W_s \le 2^m - 1$ (for $m$-bit sequence numbers), while the receiver maintains a fixed window of size $W_r = 1$. The receiver accepts only the next sequentially expected frame, discarding all out-of-order frames, and sends cumulative ACKs ($ACK_k$ acknowledges all frames up to and including $k$). If the sender's timer expires for the oldest unacknowledged frame, the sender retransmits all outstanding unacknowledged frames in the current window.
topics.exam: Maximum window size constraint: For an $m$-bit sequence number, $W_s \le 2^m - 1$ and $W_r = 1$. Channel utilization $\eta = \frac{N}{1 + 2a}$ (capped at 100%), where $N$ is sender window size.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: If $W_s = 2^m$, the protocol fails! If an entire window of ACKs is lost, the sender retransmits, but the receiver cannot distinguish whether the retransmitted frames are duplicates from the previous cycle or new frames from the next cycle.
topics.example: If $W_s = 4$ and frames 0, 1, 2, 3 are transmitted, but frame 1 is corrupted, the receiver accepts frame 0, discards frames 2 and 3 upon arrival, and repeatedly ACKs frame 0. The sender's timer expires on frame 1, forcing retransmission of frames 1, 2, and 3.
topics.q: For a 3-bit sequence number field, what is the maximum sender window size in Go-Back-N ARQ, and what is the receiver window size?
topics.a: Maximum sender window size $W_s = 2^3 - 1 = 7$. The receiver window size is strictly $W_r = 1$.

topics.title: SELECTIVE REPEAT SLIDING WINDOW ARQ
topics.sub: Independent ACKs, Receiver Buffering & Window Sizing ($W_s = W_r = 2^{m-1}$)
topics.plain: Selective Repeat fixes the wastefulness of Go-Back-N. The receiver has its own buffer window, so it happily accepts and stores out-of-order frames. It tells the sender exactly which single frame was lost (via Negative ACK or timeout), so the sender retransmits ONLY the lost frame, saving huge amounts of bandwidth.
topics.def: Selective Repeat (SR) ARQ is a pipelined protocol where both sender and receiver maintain sliding windows of size $W_s = W_r \le 2^{m-1}$ (for $m$-bit sequence numbers). The receiver accepts and buffers valid out-of-order frames falling within its window, acknowledging each frame individually with selective ACKs. The sender maintains an independent retransmission timer for each transmitted frame and retransmits only specifically unacknowledged frames upon timer expiration.
topics.exam: Window size constraint: In Selective Repeat, $W_s + W_r \le 2^m$. Since $W_s = W_r$, the maximum window size is $W_s = W_r = 2^{m-1}$. For a 4-bit sequence number ($m=4$), maximum window size is $2^{4-1} = 8$.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: If $W_s > 2^{m-1}$ in Selective Repeat, the receiver's window overlaps with the sender's sequence numbers from the previous cycle, causing the receiver to misidentify old duplicate frames as fresh new frames.
topics.example: TCP Selective Acknowledgments (SACK, RFC 2018) adopts Selective Repeat mechanics: when packets are dropped on high-speed long-distance links, SACK blocks notify the sender of received non-contiguous byte ranges so only missing segments are retransmitted.
topics.q: Why must the sender and receiver window sizes in Selective Repeat ARQ satisfy the condition $W_s = W_r \le 2^{m-1}$ for an $m$-bit sequence number?
topics.a: To prevent the receiver's window from overlapping with the sequence numbers of the previous window cycle. If $W_s + W_r > 2^m$, an unacknowledged duplicate frame could fall into the receiver's new window and be accepted as new data.

topics.title: PURE ALOHA VS SLOTTED ALOHA PROTOCOLS
topics.sub: Random Access, Vulnerable Time & Maximum Theoretical Throughput
topics.plain: ALOHA was created at the University of Hawaii for wireless island communications. In Pure ALOHA, anyone transmits whenever they feel like it; if two signals collide, both are ruined and retransmitted later. Slotted ALOHA forces everyone to wait for the tick of a clock before transmitting, cutting collision time in half and doubling throughput.
topics.def: Random access MAC protocols: 1) Pure ALOHA: stations transmit whenever they have data. Vulnerable time during which collisions can occur is $2T_{\text{fr}}$ (where $T_{\text{fr}}$ is frame transmission time). Throughput is $S = G e^{-2G}$ (where $G$ is traffic offered load); maximum throughput is $S_{\max} = 1 / (2e) \approx 0.184$ (18.4%) at $G = 0.5$. 2) Slotted ALOHA: time is discretized into synchronized slots of duration $T_{\text{fr}}$; stations must transmit only at the start of a time slot. Vulnerable time is halved to $T_{\text{fr}}$. Throughput is $S = G e^{-G}$; maximum throughput is $S_{\max} = 1 / e \approx 0.368$ (36.8%) at $G = 1.0$.
topics.exam: Vulnerable time formulas: Pure ALOHA = $2 \times T_{\text{fr}}$; Slotted ALOHA = $T_{\text{fr}}$. Maximum throughput: Pure ALOHA = $1 / (2e) \approx 18.4\%$; Slotted ALOHA = $1 / e \approx 36.8\%$.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Slotted ALOHA doubles throughput compared to Pure ALOHA, but requires strict global clock synchronization across all competing distributed stations.
topics.example: Satellite ground terminals and initial random access channels (RACH) in 4G/5G LTE cellular systems utilize slotted ALOHA variants to request initial connection setup.
topics.q: Why is the vulnerable collision time in Slotted ALOHA exactly half that of Pure ALOHA?
topics.a: In Pure ALOHA, a frame can be destroyed by another transmission starting up to one frame time before it or during its transmission, creating a vulnerable period of $2T_{\text{fr}}$. In Slotted ALOHA, transmissions are restricted to discrete slot boundaries, so collisions occur only if two stations choose the exact same slot, reducing vulnerable time to $T_{\text{fr}}$.

topics.title: CSMA/CD & MINIMUM FRAME SIZE REQUIREMENT
topics.sub: Listen Before Talking, Collision Detection & $L_{\min} \ge 2 \cdot R \cdot T_p$
topics.plain: CSMA/CD is polite conversation: listen before speaking (Carrier Sense). If quiet, talk. If someone starts talking at the exact same time, stop immediately (Collision Detection), send a jam signal, wait a random backoff time, and try again. To guarantee you detect a collision before you finish sending, the frame must be longer than the round-trip wire travel time.
topics.def: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection (CSMA/CD, IEEE 802.3) governs shared media access: 1) Carrier Sense: station monitors medium; if busy, waits (1-persistent: transmits immediately upon sensing idle). 2) Collision Detection: station listens while transmitting; if signal voltage exceeds threshold, collision is detected. 3) Jam Signal & Backoff: immediately aborts transmission, broadcasts 32-48 bit jam signal, and executes Truncated Binary Exponential Backoff ($K \in [0, 2^k - 1]$ slot times for collision $k \le 10$). To ensure detection before transmission ends, minimum frame length is $L_{\min} = 2 \cdot R \cdot T_p = 2 \cdot R \cdot (d / s)$.
topics.exam: Mandatory formula: $T_t \ge 2 T_p \implies L / R \ge 2 \cdot (d / s) \implies L_{\min} = 2 \cdot R \cdot T_p$. In standard 10 Mbps Ethernet over 2.5 km coaxial cable, $2T_p \approx 51.2\ \mu\text{s} \implies L_{\min} = 512\text{ bits} = 64\text{ bytes}$.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: If a frame is smaller than $L_{\min}$, the transmitter completes transmission and assumes success before the collision echo returns from the distant end, leaving the error entirely undetected at Layer 2.
topics.example: Legacy 10BASE5 'Thicknet' and 10BASE2 'Thinnet' shared bus Ethernet networks relied directly on CSMA/CD and 64-byte minimum frames to detect collisions across 500-meter segments.
topics.q: A 1 Gbps CSMA/CD network has a cable length of 1 km with propagation speed $2 \times 10^8$ m/s. What is the minimum frame size required for reliable collision detection?
topics.a: Propagation delay $T_p = 1000 / (2 \times 10^8) = 5\ \mu\text{s}$. Round-trip time $2T_p = 10\ \mu\text{s} = 10^{-5}\text{ s}$. Minimum frame size $L_{\min} = 2 \cdot R \cdot T_p = (10^9\text{ bps}) \times (10^{-5}\text{ s}) = 10,000\text{ bits} = 1250\text{ bytes}$.

topics.title: CSMA/CA & THE HIDDEN TERMINAL PROBLEM
topics.sub: Collision Avoidance, RTS/CTS Handshake & IEEE 802.11 Wireless LANs
topics.plain: In wireless networks, radios cannot transmit and listen at the same time (their own transmission overpowers their receiver), so collision detection is impossible. Instead, CSMA/CA avoids collisions by using interframe spaces (IFS), random backoffs, and an RTS/CTS reservation handshake to solve the hidden terminal problem.
topics.def: CSMA/CA (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Avoidance, IEEE 802.11) manages half-duplex wireless links where RF energy dynamics preclude simultaneous collision detection: 1) Interframe Spaces (DIFS, SIFS, PIFS) establish prioritized transmission windows. 2) Network Allocation Vector (NAV) maintains virtual carrier sensing by reserving channel airtime. 3) RTS/CTS Handshake: sender transmits Request-to-Send (RTS); Access Point replies with Clear-to-Send (CTS). All listening stations set NAV to silence themselves for the duration of the data and ACK exchange.
topics.exam: Hidden Terminal Problem: Node A can hear AP, Node B can hear AP, but A and B cannot hear each other due to distance/obstacles. If both transmit to AP simultaneously, their signals collide at the AP. Solution: RTS/CTS handshake (CTS broadcast by AP is heard by both A and B).
topics.trap: Exam Trap: CSMA/CD detects collisions while transmitting; CSMA/CA avoids collisions before transmitting because wireless transceivers cannot reliably listen to incoming signals while broadcasting their own signal.
topics.example: In an office Wi-Fi network, laptops on opposite sides of a conference room wall cannot sense each other's radio transmissions, but the RTS/CTS exchange with the ceiling-mounted Access Point prevents packet collisions.
topics.q: Why is CSMA/CD replaced by CSMA/CA in wireless local area networks (IEEE 802.11)?
topics.a: Because wireless transceivers operate in half-duplex; the transmit power of a station's own antenna is orders of magnitude stronger than any incoming signal, making it physically impossible to detect collisions while transmitting. Therefore, collisions must be avoided before transmission using CSMA/CA.

topics.title: ETHERNET ARCHITECTURE & IEEE 802.3 FRAME FORMAT
topics.sub: MAC Addresses, Preamble, SFD, Payload Constraints & Collision Domains
topics.plain: Ethernet is the global standard for wired LANs. Every network card has a permanent 48-bit MAC address burned into its ROM. An Ethernet frame has a preamble for clock sync, destination and source MACs, an EtherType field, a payload between 46 and 1500 bytes, and a 4-byte CRC checksum at the end.
topics.def: IEEE 802.3 Ethernet defines the physical layer and Data Link MAC sublayer for wired LANs. Frame format: Preamble (7 bytes of 10101010 for clock synchronization), Start Frame Delimiter (SFD, 1 byte 10101011), Destination MAC (6 bytes), Source MAC (6 bytes), Type/Length (2 bytes), Data Payload (46 to 1500 bytes), and Frame Check Sequence (FCS, 4-byte CRC-32). MAC addresses are 48 bits (6 bytes) long, represented as 12 hexadecimal digits (e.g., 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E), where the first 24 bits represent the Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI).
topics.exam: Ethernet frame sizing: Minimum frame length = 64 bytes (Header 14 + Payload 46 + FCS 4, excluding 8-byte preamble/SFD). Maximum frame length = 1518 bytes (Payload 1500 bytes, representing standard MTU).
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Switches break up collision domains (each switch port is its own private collision domain), but switches do NOT break up broadcast domains (broadcast frames are flooded to all ports). Routers break up broadcast domains.
topics.example: When an Ethernet switch receives a frame, it inspects the destination MAC: if known in its CAM table, it forwards out that single port; if unknown or broadcast (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF), it floods the frame across all ports except the arrival port.
topics.q: What is the minimum and maximum allowable payload (data field) size in a standard IEEE 802.3 Ethernet frame?
topics.a: Minimum payload is 46 bytes (padded with zeroes if data is smaller to guarantee the 64-byte minimum frame size). Maximum payload is 1500 bytes (the standard Maximum Transmission Unit, MTU).

quiz.q: In High-Level Data Link Control (HDLC) bit stuffing, what does the sender insert whenever it encounters five consecutive 1s in the data stream?
quiz.correctFb: To prevent user data from mimicking the 01111110 frame delimiter flag, the sender unconditionally stuffs a '0' bit after any sequence of five consecutive 1s. The receiver automatically removes any '0' bit that follows five consecutive 1s.
distractors: Inserting a '1' would generate six consecutive 1s, creating a false flag delimiter.
ESC characters are used in byte stuffing, not bit stuffing.
Inserting a flag byte would prematurely terminate the frame.

quiz.q: If the generator polynomial for a CRC error-detection system is $G(x) = x^4 + x + 1$, how many zero bits must be appended to the data block prior to modulo-2 division?
quiz.correctFb: The degree of polynomial $G(x) = x^4 + x + 1$ is 4. The number of appended zero bits equals the degree of the generator polynomial ($r = 4$).
distractors: 5 bits is the total number of coefficients in the polynomial (10011), not its degree.
3 bits is one less than the required degree.
1 bit corresponds to simple parity, not degree-4 CRC.

quiz.q: What is the maximum sender window size in the Go-Back-N ARQ protocol when sequence numbers are represented using $m$ bits?
quiz.correctFb: In Go-Back-N, the sender window cannot exceed $2^m - 1$. If it were $2^m$, the receiver could not distinguish whether an incoming frame is a duplicate retransmission or a new frame if all ACKs in a window were lost.
distractors: $2^m$ causes catastrophic sequence ambiguity when an entire window of ACKs is lost.
$2^{m-1}$ is the maximum window size for Selective Repeat ARQ.
$m$ is merely the bit width of the sequence number field.

quiz.q: For a 4-bit sequence number field ($m = 4$), what is the maximum sender window size in the Selective Repeat ARQ protocol?
quiz.correctFb: In Selective Repeat, window sizes must satisfy $W_s = W_r \le 2^{m-1}$. For $m = 4$, the maximum sender window size is $2^{4-1} = 2^3 = 8$.
distractors: 15 ($2^m - 1$) is the window limit for Go-Back-N, which causes sequence overlap in Selective Repeat.
16 ($2^m$) would cause severe duplicate frame misidentification.
7 is $2^3 - 1$, which is unnecessary since $2^3 = 8$ is fully supported.

quiz.q: In a Stop-and-Wait ARQ link, the transmission delay $T_t = 1\text{ ms}$ and the one-way propagation delay $T_p = 2\text{ ms}$. Assuming an error-free channel and negligible processing and ACK transmission times, what is the channel efficiency?
quiz.correctFb: Parameter $a = T_p / T_t = 2 / 1 = 2$. Channel efficiency $\eta = 1 / (1 + 2a) = 1 / (1 + 2 \times 2) = 1 / 5 = 0.20 = 20\%$.
distractors: 50% incorrectly calculates $1 / (1 + a) = 1 / 3$ or assumes half-duplex splitting without round-trip.
25% corresponds to $a = 1.5$.
33.3% mistakenly omits the return propagation trip ($1 / (1 + a)$).

quiz.q: Why does the CSMA/CD protocol require that frame transmission time be at least twice the one-way propagation delay ($T_t \ge 2 T_p$)?
opts: To allow the receiver enough time to compute the CRC-32 checksum.
To ensure that the transmitting station is still sending when a collision signal from the farthest node returns.
To guarantee that the channel reaches 100% theoretical utilization.
To allow the station to transmit an acknowledgment frame immediately.
quiz.correctFb: In the worst-case scenario, a collision occurs at the far end of the cable just before the frame arrives ($t \approx T_p$). The collision signal takes another $T_p$ to travel back to the sender. To detect this collision, the sender must still be actively transmitting when the collision fragment arrives at $t = 2T_p$.
distractors: CRC computation occurs in hardware on the fly and is unrelated to link propagation time.
CSMA/CD channel utilization is strictly below 100% due to collisions and backoff.
Acknowledgments in CSMA/CD Ethernet are handled at higher layers, not in the CSMA/CD MAC loop.

quiz.q: What are the maximum theoretical channel throughput values for Pure ALOHA and Slotted ALOHA, respectively?
quiz.correctFb: Pure ALOHA has maximum throughput $S_{\max} = 1 / (2e) \approx 0.184$ (18.4%) at offered traffic $G = 0.5$. Slotted ALOHA halves the vulnerable period, yielding $S_{\max} = 1 / e \approx 0.368$ (36.8%) at $G = 1.0$.
distractors: Inverts the throughputs of Pure and Slotted ALOHA.
50% and 100% are impossible under random access contention.
Arbitrary values that underestimate theoretical ALOHA bounds.

quiz.q: In IEEE 802.11 wireless networks, which mechanism is specifically used to resolve the Hidden Terminal Problem?
quiz.correctFb: The RTS/CTS handshake resolves the hidden terminal problem because the Access Point's CTS broadcast reaches all stations within range, informing hidden nodes to set their Network Allocation Vector (NAV) and withhold transmissions.
distractors: Exponential backoff resolves contention after collision, but cannot prevent collisions between hidden terminals.
Manchester encoding is a physical layer line coding technique.
CRC detects bit corruption, but cannot prevent collisions.

quiz.q: In Ethernet CSMA/CD Binary Exponential Backoff, after 3 consecutive collisions ($k = 3$), from what range of slot times does the station randomly choose its backoff delay?
quiz.correctFb: In Binary Exponential Backoff, after collision $k$, the delay is randomly chosen from $0 \le K \le 2^k - 1$. For $k = 3$, the range is $0$ to $2^3 - 1 = 0$ to $7$ slot times.
distractors: 0 to 3 corresponds to $k = 2$ ($2^2 - 1 = 3$).
0 to 15 corresponds to $k = 4$ ($2^4 - 1 = 15$).
The backoff algorithm includes 0 as a possible choice and caps at $2^k - 1$.

quiz.q: What is the minimum total frame size required for a standard IEEE 802.3 Ethernet frame (including MAC headers and FCS, but excluding the preamble and SFD)?
quiz.correctFb: The minimum total Ethernet frame length is 64 bytes (consisting of 14 bytes MAC header, 46 bytes minimum payload, and 4 bytes FCS). If the payload is less than 46 bytes, pad bytes are added.
distractors: 46 bytes is the minimum payload size, not the total frame size.
1500 bytes is the maximum payload size (standard MTU).
512 bits (64 bytes) is the frame size in bits, but the option says 512 bytes.

bossChallenges.scenario: [10 MARKS] University Exam Question: Formally analyze the principles of error detection and flow control at the Data Link Layer. Formulate the mathematical mechanics of Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) error detection using polynomial modulo-2 arithmetic, provide an exhaustive comparative analysis between Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat sliding window ARQ protocols with sequence number window constraints, and prove why CSMA/CD enforces the minimum frame size condition L_min >= 2 * R * T_p.
rubric: Criterion 1 (2.5 Marks): Complete mathematical formulation of CRC generation and verification using Galois Field GF(2) XOR arithmetic, specifying degree r zeros appended and burst error detection capabilities.

Criterion 2 (2.5 Marks): Detailed architectural comparison of Go-Back-N versus Selective Repeat ARQ, including sender/receiver window sizes (2^m - 1 vs 2^(m-1)), cumulative vs independent ACKs, and receiver buffer requirements.

Criterion 3 (2.5 Marks): Rigorous analytical proof and space-time diagram derivation of the CSMA/CD minimum frame size condition (T_t >= 2 * T_p), explaining worst-case collision echo detection at t = 2 * T_p.
Criterion 4 (2.5 Marks): Analysis of collision resolution via Binary Exponential Backoff and explanation of how the RTS/CTS handshake in CSMA/CA resolves the hidden terminal problem in wireless LANs.

bossChallenges.scenario: [5 MARKS] Practical Problem-Solving Scenario: A 100 Mbps CSMA/CD Ethernet campus network spanning a 2 km cable run with signal propagation velocity of 2 * 10^8 m/s is experiencing undetected packet collisions and frequent silent data corruption. A network engineer suspects that undersized frames are escaping the collision detection window. Determine the absolute minimum frame size required to eliminate this defect, diagnose why 64-byte frames fail under these parameters, and formulate an architectural remedy.
rubric: Criterion 1 (1.25 Marks): Accurate numerical computation of one-way propagation delay (10 microseconds) and round-trip collision window (20 microseconds).
Criterion 2 (1.25 Marks): Calculation of the required minimum frame size (2000 bits = 250 bytes) using the formula L_min = 2 * R * T_p.

Criterion 3 (1.25 Marks): Diagnostic justification explaining why standard 64-byte (512-bit) frames finish transmitting in 5.12 microseconds, leaving the transmitter unable to detect collisions occurring after that time.
Criterion 4 (1.25 Marks): Practical remediation strategy recommending packet padding, frame bursting / carrier extension, or segmenting the network into switched full-duplex collision domains.

topics.title: IPV4 ADDRESSING & CLASSFUL ARCHITECTURE
topics.sub: Classes A, B, C, D, E, Subnet Masks & Special Address Blocks
topics.plain: Every machine on the internet needs a 32-bit address written as 4 numbers separated by dots (like 192.168.1.1). Originally, IPs were divided into fixed classes based on the first few bits: Class A for huge corporations, Class B for universities, Class C for small businesses, Class D for multicasting, and Class E for scientific experiments.
topics.def: IPv4 addresses are 32-bit logical identifiers expressed in dotted-decimal notation ($4 \times 8$ octets). Classful addressing partitions the $2^{32}$ address space into 5 classes: Class A (first octet 0-127, leading bit 0, default mask /8 or 255.0.0.0, 16M hosts), Class B (128-191, leading bits 10, default mask /16 or 255.255.0.0, 65k hosts), Class C (192-223, leading bits 110, default mask /24 or 255.255.255.0, 254 hosts), Class D (224-239, leading bits 1110, multicast), and Class E (240-255, leading bits 1111, experimental).
topics.exam: Recognize leading bits instantly: Class A = 0... (0-127), Class B = 10... (128-191), Class C = 110... (192-223), Class D = 1110... (224-239), Class E = 1111... (240-255). Loopback address 127.0.0.1 is reserved.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Classful addressing wasted vast address space (e.g., getting a Class B block allocated 65,536 addresses even if an organization only needed 500), leading directly to CIDR adoption.
topics.example: RFC 1918 Private IP ranges: 10.0.0.0/8 (Class A private), 172.16.0.0/12 (Class B private), and 192.168.0.0/16 (Class C private) are non-routable on the public internet and translated via NAT.
topics.q: What are the first octet range, leading bit pattern, and default subnet mask for an IPv4 Class B network?
topics.a: First octet range: 128 to 191; leading bit pattern: binary 10; default subnet mask: 255.255.0.0 (or /16 prefix).

topics.title: CLASSLESS INTER-DOMAIN ROUTING (CIDR) & VLSM
topics.sub: Prefix Notation, Subnet ID, Directed Broadcast & Usable Host Math
topics.plain: CIDR throws away rigid classes. Instead of fixed /8, /16, or /24 boundaries, a slash notation like /27 means the first 27 bits are the network ID, leaving 32 - 27 = 5 bits for hosts. This allows Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) to carve networks to exact sizes without wasting IP addresses.
topics.def: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR, RFC 1519) replaces classful networks with arbitrary prefix lengths expressed as IP/n, where $n$ (0 to 32) indicates the count of contiguous network bits. For a prefix of length $n$, the number of available host bits is $h = 32 - n$. Total IP addresses = $2^h$; Usable assignable host addresses = $2^h - 2$ (subtracting the all-0s Network Address and all-1s Directed Broadcast Address). Subnet ID is computed via bitwise AND: $\text{Subnet ID} = \text{IP} \ \&\ \text{Subnet Mask}$.
topics.exam: Mandatory exam formulas: Host bits $h = 32 - n$. Total IPs = $2^h$. Usable hosts = $2^h - 2$. Subnet address: set all $h$ host bits to 0. Broadcast address: set all $h$ host bits to 1.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Always remember to subtract 2 for usable hosts! If asked 'how many devices can be connected to a /28 subnet', the answer is $2^4 - 2 = 14$ devices, NOT 16.
topics.example: Given IP 192.168.10.75/26: $n = 26 \implies h = 6$ host bits. Total IPs = $2^6 = 64$. Subnet mask = 255.255.255.192. Subnet ID = 192.168.10.64. Usable host range = 192.168.10.65 to 192.168.10.126. Broadcast address = 192.168.10.127.
topics.q: For the subnet 200.50.10.0/28, determine: 1) Subnet mask, 2) Total number of usable host IP addresses, 3) The directed broadcast address.
topics.a: 1) Subnet mask = 255.255.255.240 (28 ones). 2) Host bits $h = 32 - 28 = 4 \implies 2^4 - 2 = 14$ usable hosts. 3) Broadcast address = 200.50.10.15.

topics.title: IPV4 DATAGRAM HEADER & PACKET FRAGMENTATION
topics.sub: Header Fields, MTU, DF/MF Flags & Fragment Offset Calculations
topics.plain: An IPv4 datagram has a minimum 20-byte header containing source IP, destination IP, Time-to-Live (TTL), and fragmentation controls. If a packet is larger than the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) of an outgoing cable (e.g. 1500 bytes on Ethernet), intermediate routers chop it into smaller fragments and use the Fragment Offset to reassemble it at the destination.
topics.def: The IPv4 datagram header is 20 to 60 bytes long (standard 20 bytes when IHL = 5). Fragmentation fields: 1) Identification (16 bits): uniquely tags all fragments of an original datagram. 2) Flags (3 bits): Reserved (bit 0), Don't Fragment (DF, bit 1: if set and packet > MTU, router discards packet and returns ICMP 'Fragmentation Needed'), More Fragments (MF, bit 2: 1 for all fragments except the last, which has MF = 0). 3) Fragment Offset (13 bits): specifies the position of fragment data relative to the original unfragmented payload, measured strictly in 8-byte (64-bit) units.
topics.exam: Fragment Offset Formula: $\text{Offset} = \frac{\text{Starting Payload Byte Index}}{8}$. Because the offset field is scaled by 8, each fragment's payload size (except the last) MUST be an exact multiple of 8 bytes!
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Intermediate routers fragment packets, but reassembly is performed EXCLUSIVELY at the final destination host. Intermediate routers never reassemble fragments.
topics.example: A 4000-byte datagram (20B header + 3980B data) reaches an MTU = 1500B link. Frag 1: 20B header, 1480B data (divisible by 8), MF=1, Offset=0. Frag 2: 20B header, 1480B data, MF=1, Offset = 1480/8 = 185. Frag 3: 20B header, 1020B data, MF=0, Offset = (1480+1480)/8 = 2960/8 = 370.
topics.q: An IPv4 datagram with 20 bytes header and 2400 bytes data enters a network with an MTU of 1000 bytes. What are the payload size, MF flag, and Fragment Offset for the second fragment?
topics.a: Max payload per 1000-byte MTU = $1000 - 20 = 980$ bytes; largest multiple of 8 $\le 980$ is 976 bytes. Fragment 1 has 976 bytes (Offset 0, MF=1). Fragment 2 carries 976 bytes, MF=1, and Fragment Offset = $976 / 8 = 122$.

topics.title: ADDRESS RESOLUTION PROTOCOL (ARP)
topics.sub: Resolving Logical IP to Physical MAC, ARP Cache & Gratuitous ARP
topics.plain: Computers know the destination IP address, but physical network switches only understand MAC addresses. ARP is shouting into a crowded room: 'Who has IP 192.168.1.5? Tell me your MAC address!' The question is broadcast to everyone, but only the owner whispers back their MAC address in a private unicast reply.
topics.def: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP, RFC 826) maps a 32-bit logical IPv4 address to a 48-bit physical MAC address on a local broadcast domain. Operation: 1) Sender checks its local ARP Cache table; if absent, it broadcasts an ARP Request frame (Dest MAC: FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, EtherType: 0x0806). 2) Every host on the subnet receives the frame, but only the host matching the Target IP sends an ARP Reply frame directly to the sender via unicast. 3) Sender updates its ARP cache with an expiration TTL timer. Gratuitous ARP is an unsolicited announcement used to detect duplicate IP addresses.
topics.exam: ARP message flow: ARP Request is BROADCAST (Layer 2 address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF); ARP Reply is UNICAST directly to the requester's MAC address.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: ARP operates strictly within a single local broadcast domain (LAN). A host cannot send an ARP request across a router; to reach an external IP, the host resolves the MAC address of its Default Gateway.
topics.example: When typing `ping 192.168.1.1`, the OS first checks `arp -a`. If no entry exists for 192.168.1.1, the network stack pauses ICMP, broadcasts an ARP Request, learns `c0:25:e9:12:34:56`, caches it, and transmits the ICMP echo.
topics.q: Why is an ARP Request transmitted as a broadcast frame whereas the corresponding ARP Reply is sent as a unicast frame?
topics.a: An ARP Request is broadcast because the sender does not know which physical host owns the target IP address. The ARP Reply is unicast because the target host learned the requester's MAC address directly from the incoming ARP Request header.

topics.title: INTERNET CONTROL MESSAGE PROTOCOL (ICMP)
topics.sub: Error Reporting, Query Messages, Ping & Traceroute Mechanics
topics.plain: IP is unreliable and doesn't complain when packets are dropped. ICMP is the diagnostic feedback system: it reports errors back to the sender when a destination is unreachable, a packet gets too old (TTL expires), or a redirect is needed. Tools like `ping` and `traceroute` rely entirely on ICMP.
topics.def: Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP, RFC 792) provides feedback on network communication problems, encapsulated directly inside IPv4 datagrams (IP protocol field = 1). Two categories: 1) Error Reporting Messages: Type 3 (Destination Unreachable: host, network, or port unreachable), Type 4 (Source Quench / congestion), Type 11 (Time Exceeded: TTL drops to 0 in transit or fragment reassembly timeout), Type 12 (Parameter Problem). 2) Query Messages: Type 8 (Echo Request) and Type 0 (Echo Reply), utilized by the `ping` utility.
topics.exam: Traceroute mechanism: Sends packets with incrementally increasing TTL values: Packet 1 has TTL=1 (first router decrements to 0, drops packet, returns ICMP Type 11 Time Exceeded); Packet 2 has TTL=2, and so forth, mapping each router along the path.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: ICMP reports errors only to the original source IP; ICMP error messages are NEVER generated in response to an existing ICMP error message, to avoid infinite broadcast storms.
topics.example: When a router receives a packet with TTL = 1, it decrements TTL to 0, discards the packet, and generates an ICMP Type 11 Code 0 (Time-to-Live exceeded in transit) message back to the source IP.
topics.q: How does the `traceroute` command exploit the IPv4 Time-To-Live (TTL) field and ICMP messages to map the path to a destination host?
topics.a: `traceroute` sends packets starting with TTL = 1, then TTL = 2, and so on. Each successive router decrements the TTL by 1; when TTL hits 0, that router drops the packet and returns an ICMP Type 11 (Time Exceeded) message, revealing its IP address to the sender.

topics.title: DISTANCE VECTOR ROUTING & ROUTING INFORMATION PROTOCOL (RIP)
topics.sub: Bellman-Ford Algorithm, Periodic Vector Exchanges & RIP Characteristics
topics.plain: Distance Vector routing is 'routing by rumor'. Every router periodically tells its immediate neighbors its total estimated distance to every known network. Routers use the Bellman-Ford equation to update their tables if a neighbor offers a cheaper path.
topics.def: Distance Vector Routing is an asynchronous, iterative routing algorithm based on the distributed Bellman-Ford algorithm: $D_x(y) = \min_v \{c(x,v) + D_v(y)\}$, where $D_x(y)$ is the least cost from router $x$ to destination $y$, $c(x,v)$ is the cost to neighbor $v$, and $D_v(y)$ is $v$'s advertised cost to $y$. Routing Information Protocol (RIP, RFC 1058/2453) is an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) implementing Distance Vector: uses hop count as metric (each link cost = 1), broadcasts routing tables every 30 seconds via UDP port 520, and defines infinity as 16 hops.
topics.exam: Key RIP parameters: Metric = Hop count (maximum 15 hops; 16 hops = infinity / unreachable). Update timer = 30 seconds. Transport = UDP port 520.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Distance vector algorithms have slow convergence and suffer from the Count-to-Infinity problem when link costs increase or links fail.
topics.example: If router A has direct neighbor B (cost 1) and B advertises cost 3 to reach network Z, router A calculates cost to Z as $1 + 3 = 4$ through next-hop B.
topics.q: In the Routing Information Protocol (RIP), what is the maximum permissible hop count, and what specific hop count value signifies that a network is unreachable (infinity)?
topics.a: The maximum valid path metric is 15 hops. A hop count of 16 represents infinity, indicating that the destination network is unreachable.

topics.title: COUNT-TO-INFINITY PROBLEM & ROUTING LOOP REMEDIES
topics.sub: Routing Loops, Split Horizon, Poison Reverse & Hold-Down Timers
topics.plain: When a network link breaks, distance vector routers can get caught in a vicious rumor cycle: Router A thinks Router B has a path, and Router B thinks Router A has a path. They keep adding 1 to each other's hop count, slowly counting up to infinity (16 in RIP) while packets loop forever.
topics.def: The Count-to-Infinity problem is a pathology in Distance Vector routing caused by delayed convergence following link failure, where adjacent nodes exchange stale routes forming a routing loop that increments hop counts until reaching infinity. Remedies include: 1) Maximum Metric: bounds infinity to a small integer (16 in RIP) to terminate loops. 2) Split Horizon: a router does not advertise a route back out the same interface from which it learned that route. 3) Poison Reverse: a router explicitly advertises a distance of infinity (metric 16) for a route back to the neighbor from whom it learned that route. 4) Hold-Down Timers: suppresses route updates for a period following failure notification.
topics.exam: Split Horizon Rule: Never tell a neighbor about a route you learned from that neighbor. Split Horizon with Poison Reverse: Tell the neighbor about that route, but set its metric to INFINITY (16).
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Split Horizon prevents 2-node routing loops, but CANNOT prevent loops involving 3 or more routers (e.g., A -> B -> C -> A loops).
topics.example: If link between B and network X fails, B sets cost to X = $\infty$. But if Split Horizon is disabled, A tells B 'I can reach X with cost 2'. B updates table to cost 3 via A; A then updates to cost 4 via B, counting up to 16.
topics.q: What is the difference between standard Split Horizon and Split Horizon with Poison Reverse in distance vector routing?
topics.a: Standard Split Horizon completely suppresses advertising a route back out of the interface through which it was learned. Split Horizon with Poison Reverse actively advertises that route back to the source, but explicitly marks its cost as infinity (hop count 16) to immediately eliminate ambiguity.

topics.title: LINK STATE ROUTING & OPEN SHORTEST PATH FIRST (OSPF)
topics.sub: Dijkstra's SPF Algorithm, LSA Flooding, Areas & Rapid Convergence
topics.plain: Instead of trading rumors, Link State routers build a complete, identical map of the entire network. Every router floods Link State Advertisements (LSAs) describing its immediate neighbors. Once every router has the full map, each independently runs Dijkstra's algorithm to find the absolute shortest path tree.
topics.def: Link State routing requires every node to discover its neighbors, measure link costs, construct Link State Packets (LSPs/LSAs), flood them reliably to all nodes in the routing domain, and execute Dijkstra's Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm ($O(V^2)$ or $O(E + V \log V)$) on the resulting global topology database. Open Shortest Path First (OSPF, RFC 2328) is an open-standard Link State IGP: runs directly over IP (protocol 89), uses 100 Mbps / bandwidth as cost metric, supports hierarchical Areas centered on Backbone Area 0, and converges within milliseconds with zero count-to-infinity risk.
topics.exam: OSPF characteristics: Protocol = IP protocol 89 (no TCP/UDP). Metric = Cost (inversely proportional to bandwidth: $\text{Cost} = 10^8 / \text{Bandwidth}$). Hierarchical design requires Area 0 (Backbone Area) connecting all non-backbone areas.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: Link State routers do not exchange entire routing tables like RIP; they flood Link State Advertisements (LSAs) only when a link state changes or on a long refresh timer (30 minutes).
topics.example: In an enterprise campus network, multiple OSPF areas connect to Area 0. When an optical fiber link is severed, the connected router floods an LSA within milliseconds, prompting all routers to recompute Dijkstra's tree without routing loops.
topics.q: What two fundamental advantages does Link State routing (such as OSPF) have over Distance Vector routing (such as RIP)?
topics.a: 1) Rapid convergence without suffering from the Count-to-Infinity problem or routing loops; 2) Routers possess complete knowledge of the entire network topology rather than relying on second-hand distance vectors.

topics.title: BORDER GATEWAY PROTOCOL (BGP) & PATH VECTOR ROUTING
topics.sub: Autonomous Systems, AS-PATH Attribute, Policy Routing & EGP
topics.plain: BGP is the postal system that connects the entire global Internet. While OSPF routes traffic inside an organization, BGP routes packets between massive organizations and Internet Service Providers (called Autonomous Systems). It uses Path Vector routing, listing the exact list of countries/networks a packet will cross.
topics.def: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP-4, RFC 4271) is the de facto standard Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) routing traffic between distinct Autonomous Systems (AS) across the global Internet. Operating as a Path Vector protocol over reliable TCP connections (port 179), BGP advertises reachable network prefixes along with the full sequence of AS numbers traversed in the AS-PATH attribute. Loop prevention: if a BGP router receives an advertisement containing its own AS number in the AS-PATH, it immediately drops the route.
topics.exam: Key BGP attributes: Transport = TCP port 179 (connection-oriented, reliable). Algorithm = Path Vector. Loop detection = inspecting the AS-PATH attribute (discards route if local AS is listed). Primary routing criterion = commercial policies / agreements, not shortest hop count.
topics.trap: Exam Trap: BGP does NOT optimize for shortest physical delay or lowest cost; it routes based on commercial/political peering policies (e.g., 'never route US traffic through foreign carrier X').
topics.example: When an ISP (AS 13335) advertises route 1.1.1.0/24 to upstream providers, the AS-PATH lists [13335, 7018, 174]. If AS 7018 receives this path, it knows the packet must cross AS 13335 to reach the destination.
